lines.name: Shattuck Avenue line
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's electric Red Trains from its Oakland ferry pier to North Berkeley, up Adeline Street and Shattuck Avenue and through the Northbrae Tunnel to Thousand Oaks; over the Bay Bridge to San Francisco from 1939.
lines.fate_note: Replaced by Key System buses on July 26, 1941; from August 6, 1941 Key System's F trains ran over its tracks from Dwight Way to Northbrae.

route.note: Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge

sources.note: "From Oakland Pier there radiate three electric rail lines … SEVENTH STREET LINE, BERKELEY LINE, and NINTH STREET LINE."
Bridge rail service from January 15, 1939; "Except for bridge connecting tracks the rail lines serving the East Bay area were unchanged when ferry boat operation was discontinued."
The IER "will not continue the operation of its Berkeley lines after August 1, 1941" (p. 4).
Key System's substitute routes were "established on July 26, 1941 … in lieu of the operations theretofore provided by the Shattuck Avenue and Ninth Street rail lines".
The first electric train ran over the Shattuck Avenue line on a trial trip on December 22, 1911.
From 1939, Seventh Street and Alameda trains joined the old Berkeley main line at 22nd Street, and Berkeley trains at 32nd Street.
Electric service began, at first only between 9 and 4 o'clock, with steam trains removed the following week.

lines.notes: The Interurban Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific company authorized in 1936 to take over these lines (CRC D28671), ran them until 1941; the day it took over isn't sourced here. Through Northbrae to Thousand Oaks by the loop over Solano Avenue from about February 3, 1912, when service was planned to begin (San Francisco Call, February 2, 1912); the day itself isn't confirmed.

lines.name: Ninth Street line
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's electric Red Trains from its Oakland ferry pier through Emeryville and along Ninth Street in West Berkeley to Albany and Thousand Oaks; over the Bay Bridge to San Francisco from 1939.
lines.fate_note: Replaced by Key System buses on July 26, 1941.

route.note: Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge

sources.note: "From Oakland Pier there radiate three electric rail lines … SEVENTH STREET LINE, BERKELEY LINE, and NINTH STREET LINE."
Bridge rail service from January 15, 1939; "Except for bridge connecting tracks the rail lines serving the East Bay area were unchanged when ferry boat operation was discontinued."
From 1939, Seventh Street and Alameda trains joined the old Berkeley main line at 22nd Street, and Berkeley trains at 32nd Street.
Trial trip over the loop to Albany and along Ninth Street on February 2, 1912; service "within a week".

"Trains are being run on the Ninth street line separately, between the mole and Albany, between 9 and 5 o'clock, on a 40 minute schedule, principally for trial purposes"; regular loop service from "next Monday".

lines.notes: The Interurban Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific company authorized in 1936 to take over these lines (CRC D28671), ran them until 1941; the day it took over isn't sourced here. Opening: a trial train ran over the loop to Albany and along Ninth Street on February 2, 1912 (Oakland Tribune, Feb. 2), and the loop's twenty-minute service, celebrated at Albany on February 7, was inaugurated that day (Tribune, Feb. 6 and 8). But on February 12 Ninth Street trains still ran on their own, every 40 minutes from 9 to 5, "principally for trial purposes", with regular service around the loop planned for Monday, February 19 (Tribune, Feb. 12); no report of that day has been found, so the line is drawn from February 12, when a source shows it running. The San Francisco Call of February 2 had planned service from February 3; Wikipedia gives February 7, citing the Berkeley Gazette, not yet checked.

running.note: "Trains are being run on the Ninth street line separately, between the mole and Albany, between 9 and 5 o'clock, on a 40 minute schedule, principally for trial purposes."

lines.name: Seventh Street line
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's electric Red Trains from its Oakland ferry pier along Seventh Street, through East Oakland and Melrose, to Dutton Avenue in San Leandro; over the Bay Bridge to San Francisco from 1939.
lines.fate_note: Replaced from March 22, 1941 by Key System buses and an extension of its A trains, which from April 1941 ran over this line's tracks from East 14th Street to Havenscourt.

route.note: Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
From the 26th Street junction south toward 22nd Street

sources.note: "From Oakland Pier there radiate three electric rail lines … SEVENTH STREET LINE, BERKELEY LINE, and NINTH STREET LINE."
Bridge rail service from January 15, 1939; "Except for bridge connecting tracks the rail lines serving the East Bay area were unchanged when ferry boat operation was discontinued."

"an electric railway from Oakland Mole via Seventh Street, private right-of-way, Bond Street, Beck Street, Blanche Street and Bancroft Avenue to Dutton Avenue in San Leandro"; local service "on Seventh Street from Pine Street as far as Fallon Street" and "its right-of-way from Fallon Street to Melrose Station" (p. 7).
The IER would not continue the line "beyond March 1st, 1941".
Substitute service began "on March 22, 1941".
Steam trains ran on Seventh Street for the last time on the night of December 30, 1911.
From 1939, Seventh Street and Alameda trains joined the old Berkeley main line at 22nd Street, and Berkeley trains at 32nd Street.
The first regular electric trains ran on December 1, 1911 (the issue of December 2 says "today"; the dateline is garbled in the OCR), alternating with steam trains.
In September 1913 the electric trains still ended at Melrose.

lines.notes: The Interurban Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific company authorized in 1936 to take over these lines (CRC D28671), ran them until 1941; the day it took over isn't sourced here. Not yet drawn: Melrose to 106th Avenue (Bond, Beck and Blanche Streets and Bancroft Avenue, which the sources name but don't place) and the 1939–41 "Off-Line" connection from the bridge. Electric trains ran from the Oakland Pier to Melrose from December 1911, mixed with steam until December 30, 1911. When they were extended beyond Melrose to Dutton Avenue isn't sourced: the line still ended at Melrose in September 1913, so the Bancroft Avenue stretch, shown with the line's dates, opened later than it appears.

photo.author: Railway Age Gazette

lines.name: Encinal Avenue line
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's electric Red Trains across Alameda along Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue, to the Alameda Mole and its ferries; from 1939 over the Fruitvale Bridge and the Bay Bridge to San Francisco.
lines.fate_note: Replaced by Key System buses from January 18, 1941.

route.note: Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
To Fruitvale Junction, then the Fruitvale Bridge

sources.note: "From Oakland Pier there radiate three electric rail lines … SEVENTH STREET LINE, BERKELEY LINE, and NINTH STREET LINE."
Bridge rail service from January 15, 1939; "Except for bridge connecting tracks the rail lines serving the East Bay area were unchanged when ferry boat operation was discontinued."

The two Alameda lines "operate generally over parallel tracks throughout the entire residential portion of the city"; the substitute buses followed "the same streets now traversed by the rail lines east of Webster Street" (p. 9): Lincoln Avenue; Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue.
Key System buses "placed in effect January 18, 1941".
"on June 1 the Alameda line was opened" (1911); which of the two lines isn't stated.
"new electric trains from High street to the Alameda mole", from Thursday, June 1, 1911.
From 1939, Seventh Street and Alameda trains joined the old Berkeley main line at 22nd Street, and Berkeley trains at 32nd Street.
The "south side electric line" opened in part on June 1, 1911, from High Street to the Alameda mole (San Francisco Call, June 3).

lines.notes: The Interurban Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific company authorized in 1936 to take over these lines (CRC D28671), ran them until 1941; the day it took over isn't sourced here. Both Alameda lines were electrified in 1911 (CRC D33732, p. 8). Not yet drawn: the track west of Webster Street to the mole, and the east end to the Fruitvale Bridge (1939–41), which the sources don't place street by street. The June 1, 1911 opening is matched to this line because the trains ran "from High street to the Alameda mole", and the Encinal Avenue line ran to High Street (CRC D33732); no source of the day names Encinal Avenue.

photo.caption: One of the Southern Pacific's steel motor cars for its Alameda line, which opened on June 1, 1911, seen end on with its roller pantograph.
photo.author: Electric Railway Journal

lines.name: Lincoln Avenue line
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's electric Red Trains across Alameda along Lincoln Avenue, to the Alameda Mole and its ferries; from 1939 over the Fruitvale Bridge and the Bay Bridge to San Francisco.
lines.fate_note: Replaced by Key System buses from January 18, 1941.

route.note: Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
To Fruitvale Junction, then the Fruitvale Bridge

sources.note: "From Oakland Pier there radiate three electric rail lines … SEVENTH STREET LINE, BERKELEY LINE, and NINTH STREET LINE."
Bridge rail service from January 15, 1939; "Except for bridge connecting tracks the rail lines serving the East Bay area were unchanged when ferry boat operation was discontinued."

The two Alameda lines "operate generally over parallel tracks throughout the entire residential portion of the city"; the substitute buses followed "the same streets now traversed by the rail lines east of Webster Street" (p. 9): Lincoln Avenue; Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue.
Key System buses "placed in effect January 18, 1941".
"on June 1 the Alameda line was opened" (1911); which of the two lines isn't stated.
From 1939, Seventh Street and Alameda trains joined the old Berkeley main line at 22nd Street, and Berkeley trains at 32nd Street.
Announced the day before: electric service on the "horseshoe route" from the Oakland pier to the Alameda pier, by way of Lincoln Avenue, beginning the morning of December 19, 1911.

lines.notes: The Interurban Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific company authorized in 1936 to take over these lines (CRC D28671), ran them until 1941; the day it took over isn't sourced here. Both Alameda lines were electrified in 1911 (CRC D33732, p. 8). Not yet drawn: the track west of Webster Street to the mole, and the east end to the Fruitvale Bridge (1939–41), which the sources don't place street by street. The opening is the date announced the day before; no report of the day itself has been found, and earlier electric running on part of the line isn't ruled out.

lines.name: Eighteenth Street line
lines.summary: A Southern Pacific electric loop line from the Oakland Mole by Sixteenth Street Station, 18th Street and 20th Street to 14th and Franklin Streets; from 1926 down Webster Street to 2nd Street.

route.note: Down Webster Street to 2nd Street from 1926

sources.note: Service announced for March 21, 1912 (a trial ran March 11).

About 1921-26 the Eighteenth Street line ran "from Oakland Mole to 14th and Franklin Street via Sixteenth Street Station, 18th Street, 20th Street and Franklin Street. Westbound … over 21st Street and Jones Street instead of over Twentieth Street."
In 1933, "along Eighteenth, Twentieth, Twenty-first and Webster Streets, between Sixteenth Street Station and Second and Webster Streets" (2.9 miles, p. 4).
Abandoned "On the 26th day of March, 1933".

lines.notes: Opened on the day the San Francisco Call announced, March 21, 1912; no report of the day itself was found. Westbound trains used 21st Street and "Jones Street", which isn't a street in Oakland today, instead of 20th Street; that loop isn't drawn. It moved from Franklin Street to Webster Street in 1926 (CRC Decisions 14618, 16083 and 17028); the day isn't sourced, so the change is dated to the year.

lines.name: Webster Street line
lines.summary: Southern Pacific electric trains from 14th and Franklin Streets in Oakland down Webster Street and over the Harrison Street swing bridge to Alameda and the Alameda Mole.

route.note: To Alameda Pier and its ferries

sources.note: "Electric service on the Webster street road of the Southern Pacific during the entire daily schedule went into effect today" (June 29).
The Webster Street line ran "from 14th and Franklin Street to Alameda Pier via Webster Street and the Harrison Street Swing Bridge"; it was "discontinued on December 27th, 1923".
"OAKLAND (14th and Franklin)—Via Webster Street" (p. 30); double track on Webster Street, single track only "In case of emergency" (p. 32).
Southern Pacific "may cease the operation … on or after December 27th, 1923".

lines.notes: Across the estuary by the Harrison Street swing bridge (CRC Decision 17743, not the Webster Street bridge), then, as the 1915 USGS sheet draws the railroad, west along Alameda's north shore to the mole and Alameda Pier; where Webster Junction stood isn't placed. An Oakland Tribune headline of December 26, 1923, "S.P. Bridge Service to End Tonight", relayed by Wikipedia, isn't checked.

lines.name: Southern Pacific trains, Oakland Pier to San José by Elmhurst and Newark
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's last trains between Oakland and San José by the bay shore: from Oakland Pier by First St, Fruitvale and Elmhurst, then Mount Eden, Alvarado, Newark and Alviso to Santa Clara and San José; by 1941 the Oakland sections of the Coast Daylight and the Lark.
lines.fate_note: Discontinued under the Public Utilities Commission's Decision No. 59928 of April 12, 1960; the last trains ran on May 1 and, for No. 73, May 2, 1960 (Schedule Statement ST-798). Amtrak's Coast Starlight runs over it today from Elmhurst, and the Capitol Corridor from Newark south.

running.note: Nos. 250 and 255 and the Oakland Lark (74, 73), daily.

sources.note: Oakland Pier, West Oakland, Magnolia Tower, Oakland (First Street), East Oakland, Fruitvale, Elmhurst, Mulford, Robert, Russell, Mount Eden, Baumberg, Alvarado, Hall, Arden, Newark, Mowry, Albrae, Drawbridge, Alviso, Agnew, Santa Clara.
Authority to discontinue Nos. 73, 74, 250 and 255 between Oakland and San José, effective twenty days after April 12, 1960.
Last runs May 1, 1960 (74, 250, 255) and May 2 (73).

lines.notes: When the Southern Pacific's trains began to run this way, from Elmhurst instead of over the South Pacific Coast's old line from Alameda, isn't sourced; the map draws them from September 1941, the first date a source read on the page shows them (decision 20). Ends with No. 73's last run, May 2, 1960. Between San José and Santa Clara and from Newark south they ran on today's Capitol Corridor track.
